title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 16
paragraphs: While the barbarians were engaged in this work, Attaginos son of Phyrnon, a Theban, having made magnificent preparations, invited Mardonius himself and fifty of the most distinguished Persians to a feast; they came, and the dinner was held at Thebes. What follows I heard from Thersander, an Orchomenian of great reputation in Orchomenos. Thersander said that he too had been invited by Attaginos to this dinner, and fifty Thebans had also been invited; and their host did not place them to recline separately each nation by itself, but a Persian and a Theban on every couch. When dinner was over and they were drinking toasts to each other, the Persian sharing his couch, speaking in Greek, asked him where he was from, and he answered that he was of Orchomenos. The other said: “Since you have become my fellow-diner and sharer of my libation, I wish to leave behind with you a memorial of my opinion, so that you too may know in advance and be able to take such counsels as are profitable for yourself. Do you see these Persians who are feasting here, and the army we left behind encamped on the river? Of all of them, a little time from now you shall see only very few still alive.” While the Persian said this, he shed many tears, as Thersander reported; and Thersander, astonished at his words, said: “Surely, then, you should tell Mardonius and the Persians of standing after him.” He replied: “Friend, that which is destined to come from God, it is impossible for a man to avert; for no one is willing to follow good counsel, even when one speaks reasonably. Many of us Persians know these things well; yet we go with the rest, bound in the chains of necessity. And the most hateful grief of all human griefs is this: to have knowledge of the truth but no power over the outcome.” These things I heard from Thersander of Orchomenos, and in addition this: that he told them to various people at once, before the battle took place at Plataea.
